How can a clock

than a clock on

For hundreds of years,
classical mechanics reigned
over human scientific
thought, thanks to Sir
Isaac Newton.
Newton believed the universe
ran on one absolute
master clock, where a
second in London was
identical to a second
on the distant surface
of Mars.
That tidy universe came
crashing down in the
early twentieth century,
when an obscure patent
clerk in Switzerland named
Albert Einstein looked
deeper into the nature
of light.
He realized that the
speed of light in
a vacuum is an
absolute cosmic speed limit,
about 299,792 kilometers
per second, and that
it never changes.
If the speed of
light must be the
same for everyone,
then distance and time
themselves must bend to
make it so.
Ten years later,
in 1915, Einstein took
this further with his
theory of general relativity.
Space and time are
woven into a single,
four-dimensional fabric
known as spacetime.
Instead, gravity is the
geometric warping of this
fabric, caused by mass
and energy.
This warping leads to
gravitational time dilation.
When a massive object
curves spacetime, it
stretches not just the
dimensions of space,
but the rate at
which time passes.
Clocks sitting deeper within
a gravitational well run
measurably slower than
clocks resting farther
away, in weaker gravity.
You do not need
to voyage to the
edge of the galaxy
to prove that this is real.
The GPS satellites orbiting
thousands of kilometers
above our planet sit
in weaker gravity than
your phone on the ground.
Because they experience
less spacetime curvature,
the atomic clocks aboard
those satellites run about
forty-five microseconds
faster every day from
gravity alone.
If engineers did not
correct for Einstein's
equations, satellite
navigation would drift
by kilometers every single
day.
On Earth, the difference
in time flow is
measured in millionths
of a second,
because our planet is
a tiny cosmic pebble
with modest gravity.
Near a supermassive black
hole, time dilation scales
up from imperceptible
microseconds to entire
human lifetimes.
